Formulation  
- Daniel is experiencing an acute asthma exacerbation likely precipitated by a recent upper respiratory tract infection and lack of access to his inhalers, compounded by allergic predisposition (dust, hay fever). His previous severe asthma requiring intubation contributes to anxiety about current respiratory symptoms. The exacerbation is perpetuated by medication non-adherence and respiratory infection; protective factors include patient insight, previous medication compliance, and motivation to seek help.  

Mental Health Care Plan Details  

Principal Problem: Acute asthma exacerbation  
- Patient Goal(s): Regain normal breathing function; prevent further severe exacerbations and hospitalization; reduce anxiety about breathing difficulties  
- Clinical Goal(s): Reverse current asthma exacerbation; ensure adherence to inhaler therapy; monitor and manage symptoms to prevent complications  
- Actions (Patient): Collect prescribed inhalers and steroid tablets promptly; use inhalers as instructed including spacer; self-monitor symptoms; seek medical attention if worsening or ventolin use exceeds every 3 hours; rest as advised  
- Actions (Clinician/GP): Provide prescriptions for salbutamol and Clenil Modulite inhalers and spacer; prescribe short course oral steroids; educate on inhaler and spacer use; advise on warning signs requiring urgent care; provide time off work to facilitate recovery; arrange follow-up if symptoms persist or worsen  

Secondary Problem: Anxiety related to respiratory symptoms and prior severe asthma exacerbation  
- Patient Goal(s): Reduce fear related to breathing difficulty and prior intubation; feel supported and reassured regarding asthma management  
- Clinical Goal(s): Provide reassurance; monitor anxiety symptoms; educate about asthma triggers and management to improve confidence  
- Actions (Patient): Share concerns openly during consultations; utilize coping strategies for anxiety if needed  
- Actions (Clinician/GP): Provide patient education on asthma and steroids side effects; reassure patient about treatment and support; consider referral for psychological support if anxiety persists or worsens  

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention  
- Education Given: Yes. Topics covered: asthma exacerbation symptoms, inhaler and spacer technique, steroid side effects, when to seek emergency care  
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening: Increased shortness of breath, wheezing, frequent Ventolin use (>every 3 hours), chest pain, light-headedness  
- Coping Strategies: Use of inhalers as prescribed, rest, contacting health services promptly if symptoms worsen, reassurance regarding treatment  

Consent, Coordination & Review

- Copy of Mental Health Care Plan Given to Patient: Not recorded  
- Other Mental Health Professionals Involved in Patient Care: Not recorded  
- GP Acknowledgment (if completed by other MH Professional): Not applicable  
- Review Date: Not recorded; implied need for early follow-up if symptoms persist or worsen
